appraisal_events.evidence: "le peintre ridicule et pervers, adopté jadis par les Verdurin" / the Verdurin circle's old nickname "M. Biche"; the narrator feels "la déception extraordinaire" and Elstir's own face takes on "une expression de mécontentement."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's discovery that the revered Elstir was once the ridiculed painter attached to the philistine Verdurin salon produces a sharp local diminishment and open mutual disappointment.

appraisal_events.evidence: "un homme moins éminent par l'intelligence et par le coeur m'eût peut-être simplement dit au revoir un peu sèchement... Mais ce ne fut pas ainsi qu'Elstir agit avec moi; en vrai maître... il cherchait à extraire pour le meilleur enseignement des jeunes gens la part de vérité."
appraisal_events.explanation: Elstir forgoes defending his own vanity and instead offers the narrator an extended, generous reflection on youth and wisdom, an act the narrator explicitly presents as superior to how a lesser man would have reacted, decisively elevating him as a true master.

status_effects.explanation: His past as the ridiculed 'M. Biche' of the disreputable Verdurin milieu briefly discredits him in the narrator's eyes.
His wise, self-effacing, instructive response to the awkward revelation elevates him as a genuine master of intelligence and heart, outweighing the initial disappointment.

ambiguities: The initial discredit tied to Elstir's 'M. Biche'/Verdurin past is the narrator's own felt reaction in the moment; Elstir's ensuing speech implicitly reframes such youthful 'incarnations ridicules' as necessary steps toward wisdom rather than a lasting mark against him, so the negative judgment is not endorsed as a durable verdict.
